entry.title: Employer branding can't be faked
entry.content:
Ten things that worked for me, and why a thousand campaigns won’t save a bad place to work.

What is employer branding, anyway?

If branding is what people think about what your company does or builds, employer branding is what current and potential employees think about the company. The two aren’t orthogonal, but they also aren’t as directly connected as people think.

For example, I think a Tesla is a great car, but I’m not sure I’d want a boss like Musk. The best example I always give is Pornhub: a company many people would hesitate to attach their name to, whose engineering brand is actually very good.

And why do you need it? Almost always for hiring and retention. When hiring gets hard, everyone remembers employer branding, although the conversation often turns shallow (who’s performing at the Purim party, for example). It doesn’t have to be that way.

Over the last few years a number of people consulted with me about this, partly because WeWork managed to build a good employer brand in Israel (amazing work by Ron Gura, whom I learned a lot from). Here’s some of what worked for me:

1. Retention comes before hiring. Many people think employer branding should focus on recruiting, but retention is more important. What good is filling a leaking bucket? If you focus only on recruiting, the people already in the organization feel less important. That’s what you’re spending money on? Why didn’t you invest like this in me?

2. Don’t build an image for nothing. A big company can’t move fast, so there’s no point pumping that message (“we operate like a startup without the financial pressure of a startup!”) only for people to arrive, see it isn’t so, and leave after six months. Understand your real relative strengths, and double down on them.

3. Empower people. That’s how you create a culture of people who are proud of where they work. A CEO speaking at a conference is a drop in the ocean. Dozens of employees who keep writing about how interesting and fun their work is, that’s an army. And invest in people in general. It seems like good advice regardless, even if they never write a post about you.

4. Think hard about the DNA you want to create, and act on it. We had a good candidate who we asked, during her interviews, why she wanted to join us. She said she missed the feeling she’d had at another startup, where they worked into the evening and then all went out together. I told her it would be a shame for her to come, because it wouldn’t be like that with us.

5. Remember the candidates you reject. Your image forms in everyone who has interacted with the company. Do you know the biggest group that interacts with you, and that you ignore? Candidates, specifically the ones who didn’t get in (probably 90% of the pipeline). They’ll end up at another company, and your name might come up. Candidates with a bad experience will make sure to tell everyone how much you suck.

6. It’s never too early. You probably need to think about this from day one. It’s a long process, and the first people who join teach a lot about the company you’re building and shape the culture and what you stand for. Employer branding is more and more activities whose fruits you sometimes see only after months or years.

7. Can’t talk about what you do? Focus on the goal. Focus on the mission rather than the specific solution. Our product changed a lot, but our goal, helping developers grow professionally in a playful way, stayed relatively stable.

8. People. People. People. People want to work with good people, who are fun to be around and who they can learn from. Few people are interested in insurance, but Lemonade has amazing people. What you do is nice, but for many people it isn’t the most critical thing, and who their manager is matters more. Invest in bringing in good people, from the start.

9. Share. You’re not working on the atomic bomb here. Nothing will happen if everyone sees how you’re progressing. Share failures too, because no company is all roses. The more information people have, the shorter the due diligence in interviews, and the fewer false positives.

10. More than anything, you can’t fake it. If the company isn’t a good place to work, a thousand campaigns won’t fix that. If there are toxic people, they’ll poison everyone who comes. And if there are no big, interesting problems, maybe you don’t need hundreds of people who are all seniors.

This post started as a thread on X and later a LinkedIn post.

entry.title: There is no recipe
entry.content:
I replaced all the exclamation marks at the end of my sentences with question marks.

A lot of people ask me why I don’t share about Wilco anymore, and it’s a question I find a bit hard to answer.

There are the obvious reasons, which I learned the hard way:

  1. The bigger a company gets, the slower things move, so not much changes.
  2. We’re not alone anymore. There’s a team, investors and customers, so you have to censor yourself more.
  3. When there are fewer successes, there’s less to share.

But I want to write about the fourth reason.

The programmer’s way

The hardest part for me, as a programmer entering the world of entrepreneurship, was that there was no “recipe” I could follow.

As a programmer, when I hit a problem I go do research. I read books, talk to my network, learn from past cases. After collecting data you quickly start seeing patterns. The solution space turns out to be pretty closed, and you understand the pros and cons of each alternative.

That’s how I thought it would be when we started thinking about raising money. We weren’t sure at all when the right time was, or how much. So I started asking a lot of entrepreneurs who’d been there, experienced people I hold in high regard, some of whom had built big companies.

To my surprise, I simply got a huge and contradictory amount of opinions:

  • Stay at your job as long as possible so you can work with a clear head. Leave as soon as possible, because it looks bad to investors and you have to give 200%.
  • Take a few months to work on a product and then raise. Don’t build anything, it’s easier to raise on just an idea.
  • Raise the bare minimum so you come into the next round strong. Don’t you dare raise small, funds love a clean cap table.
  • Hire an advisor to take care of it. Don’t you dare bring in someone who’ll take a percentage.
  • Bring as many customers as you can, even for free. Free customers aren’t interesting, one paying customer beats ten free ones.
  • Emphasize the solution. The solution doesn’t matter, emphasize the problem. Emphasize the team, everything’s going to change later anyway.
  • Don’t talk to funds at all. Don’t talk to angels at all. Start spreading the word.

The peak was when a very close mentor warmly suggested we close a customer from abroad, to show how strong we are for bringing in a customer from outside our network. We managed to close one. A few weeks later we presented to one of the strongest people in Israeli high tech, and he simply scolded us for looking for customers abroad, because it actually showed how weak our network was.

I walked out of that conversation in shock. Then I remembered a tip I got from Ron Gura and Nimrod Priell, on two separate occasions: you can read and learn until tomorrow, but in entrepreneurship you just have to try and develop instincts. It’s a muscle you have to train.

So we started letting go, trusting ourselves more, and gave ourselves permission to be wrong.

I was an idiot

When I started this journey two years ago (it feels like a decade), I had a very well-formed idea of how a startup should be run. I’d read all the books and listened to all the podcasts. I’d even been in a company or two from the very beginning. I thought I was coming with a recipe and just had to execute it.

I was an idiot.

I don’t think there’s a single thing I once believed to be true about entrepreneurship that I haven’t changed my mind about. The path to growth, how to build a team, what to do to bring in customers, how to build the product. If there’s one thing I’ve learned, mostly in the last year, it’s that I don’t know anything. A great lesson in humility, delivered by a flying kick.

Since then I walk around the world not believing anything professional, from anyone. If someone speaks with confidence, I scorn them. My whole foundation was shaken. As far as I’m concerned, every piece of advice I read was written by ChatGPT with a hallucination.

Obviously that’s an exaggeration too, but I sit at meetups where founders recite mantras and I want to stand up and say, “Glad it worked for you in 2017. I tried what you said, I suggest nobody does it, it doesn’t work, gentlemen.”

I was so captive to the concept that I convinced myself there was a direct link between what we did and the outcome, when in practice things bigger than us plus luck played a much bigger role. As a deterministic person, that’s discouraging. It’s like looking at an A/B test with two opposite results. It makes you lose faith in the method.

Back to natural size

So this past year has mostly made me lower my voice. I don’t have the privilege of speaking unequivocally. I replaced all the exclamation marks at the end of my sentences with question marks. When people come to me for advice I hedge, and when an issue comes up I analyze it, but I always understand that a lot of it doesn’t depend on what I do.

At the end of the day it brings you down to your natural size, and it makes me, at least, focus on just doing. And then doing more and more and more, until at some point something hits, and I won’t know why. So I’ll just keep going, and focus more on doing and less on talking.

This post started as two threads on X, from 2021 and 2023.

entry.title: Startups don't have to burn you out
entry.content:
If you work like a crazy person, eventually you go crazy.

In the last few weeks I had several conversations with people I’d be happy to have working with me. They said they’re afraid to make the move, mainly because of what it would do to their work-life balance. So here’s how we see it, and why I think it doesn’t have to be that way.

How I burned out

Let’s start many years ago. Around 2012 I joined a startup as the first employee, in my twenties and with no kids. I basically had nothing much to do in life other than go to a Maccabi game once a week. The two founders had already been working for about half a year without salaries, and I joined right after the fundraise.

It was a great time. I learned a ton and grew professionally in an exceptional way. On the other hand, work was my life. I worked something like 12 hours a day and didn’t have much room for anything else.

It’s important to say that nobody told me to stay, and nobody made a face when I left at 5 (for a Maccabi game). It just worked that way, by inertia.

This also wasn’t a two-week crunch before a release, or a month for some event. We ran like that for more than three years. I didn’t feel it was bad (I’m learning and growing!), and nobody was there to tell me to stop. Even when my eldest daughter was born it didn’t change. A few days at home and, hop, back to it.

Half a year later everything started to collapse. A chain of unrelated events, a family crisis, health problems with my daughter and a deal that fell through, all drained together, and I simply crashed.

I couldn’t get out of bed. I spent whole months either at playgrounds or in hospitals. In hindsight I understood it was burnout. In real time it was just 0% energy.

It was a formative event for me. Since then I’ve been very careful about a few rules to protect this, and more than that, it’s important for me to pass it on to the people working with me and to create a balanced work environment.

Because that’s the thing about work-life balance: it’s like sand, and it will easily slip through your fingers if you don’t pay attention.

What I do now

Since then I make sure to have at least one short day, and the vast majority of the time I close the computer at 6pm. Even in more stressful periods. Even when I was in leadership positions.

I can do that because the group plans ahead, understands that resources are limited, and tries to get the most out of them assuming people work 8 hours a day (or even less).

There’s a lot to say about how you do each thing: good communication, pedantic planning, the ability to adjust while moving, people raising flags often. But it starts with the basic constraint. We have X person-hours, and that won’t move, no matter what. You can’t play with those numbers. Now let’s see what we can do, and when.

That conversation is what we started from as founders. The three of us left very comfortable (and well-paid) jobs, we all have kids, we all have hobbies, and we knew we weren’t going to hurt that. We say it out loud to investors too: we’re going to kill ourselves for this every day, and then we’re going to go help with bath time.

How it usually happens

What usually happens in startups looks like this. The founders, who are very invested, work very hard. The beginning of a company is chaotic and there’s always something to do. More people join and carry on the same way, by inertia.

Then the first version comes out, not exactly on time of course (that’s software projects for you), and everyone works very hard on it, and that’s how the snowball grows. More employees join an existing reality, see that this is how things work here and that you can’t get ahead without working 12 hours a day. And nobody stops to think.

It doesn’t have to be this way.

That’s why I struggle when people say you can’t do a startup without working like crazy. If you work like crazy, eventually you go crazy. If you own 40% of the company, fine, you’re the one who went all in. But if you own 0.04%? I don’t expect you to go crazy. We’re in a marathon here, and everyone has to save their breath.

People need to care: about the company, the customers, the people, the product. In a startup especially, I think that’s a must. But you can’t exploit it. And it can’t be that if someone goes on a three-day vacation, everything collapses. If that’s the situation, the company has much bigger problems and it’s an unhealthy work environment. In the long run, I have to solve that.

I’m not fooling myself. A startup is much more stressful and demanding than a big company. In a big company, when balls get dropped, there’s often a support network that catches them (or nobody cares that the ball fell). The challenge is to create an environment where even in a startup, when balls fall (and they will), it isn’t a catastrophe.

Is it possible? I think (and hope) so.

What I do know is that this time I’ll take a step back if I see us starting to slide down that slope, and for that we’ve set up a support network of people who will say “stop” in time.

entry.title: Evaluating startup ideas on two axes
entry.content:
For choosing a workplace, or for when a friend at a bar has “the next unicorn, bro”.

I should be working on my talk for Reversim, so of course I’m procrastinating and writing this instead.

This isn’t a personal story, it’s a framework that helps me evaluate ideas. I should say I didn’t read about it anywhere. It’s just something I slowly built for myself in my head, out of observation and past experience.

Every startup begins with a team that has to come together around an idea (not necessarily in that order). As I’ve said before, I don’t think the idea is that important, and it doesn’t need to be airtight. On the contrary, you need some flexibility, because the idea is going to change a thousand times.

But what do you do when you’re thinking about an idea? At first a lot of ideas come up, each of which could take the company somewhere else. They’ll all look genius at first, and an hour later they’ll look stupid.

To help me evaluate an idea, I put it on a set of axes. The X axis is the size of the market, and the Y axis is the difficulty.

Difficulty of solving the problem can be technological (very specific knowledge), procedural (FDA approvals) or about market penetration (getting people to host strangers in their homes). Difficulty is relative, and what’s hard for one team can be easy for another.

Market size is usually measured as total addressable market (TAM), or as we say in Israel: “how much money is in there?” For example, there are hundreds of millions of mobile users, but none of them spends too much on apps. On the other hand, there aren’t many people working in enterprise security, but everyone knows there’s a sea of money there.

Now let’s map each quadrant. To quote my partner On Freund: “the interesting part is on the diagonals”.

Quadrant 1: hard problem, huge market

These are the classic VC companies. There’s a huge market waiting for a solution, and if the team can solve this hard problem, there’s bonanza potential.

Examples: DoorDash (operations at scale), Stitch Fix (an algorithm for a recommendation engine that works), Intuit (bureaucracy).

  • Pros: if you make it through the difficulty (usually a big “if”), there’s potential for big money.
  • Cons: you need to find someone who’ll believe in you and put money on you, commitment, long cycles.

There’s also a subgroup here: super hard problems in an enormous market. Because of the nature of these problems, there’s an underserved audience just waiting for a solution. The players here are the tech giants, because they have tons of money, talent and influence, and they’re thirsty for more market share.

Examples: robots (Amazon), smart cities (Google), internet in third-world countries (Facebook).

Quadrant 2: hard problem, small market

On paper this quadrant isn’t worth the investment, but companies here are betting on a market that keeps growing. The rationale is that if and when the market gets there, they’ll be first in line with the knowledge and the product.

Examples: Beyond Meat (bet on the vegetarian trend), Twilio (SaaS developers), the first mobile developers.

  • Pros: the thrill of being pioneers, and if you solve it but the market doesn’t get there, potential for a good acquisition.
  • Cons: a big bet (on both the solution and the market), and you really have to time the market (being early isn’t good either).

Quadrant 3: easy problem, small market

Classic bootstrap products. DHH says that to reach a million dollars in annual revenue, all you need is 1,000 users paying you $100 a month. Numbers like that are something you can bring in from the garage. On the other hand, funds will shut the door as soon as they see them.

Examples: Basecamp, and thousands of companies you haven’t heard of because they make great money and save on PR.

  • Pros: no big investment or commitment at the start, you can begin while working, passive income.
  • Cons: finding users is very hard, and the moment you’re onto something, someone will copy the product.

Quadrant 4: easy problem, big market

Supposedly the holy grail. But as my economics lecturer said (I didn’t study economics): if they told me there was $100 on the floor, I wouldn’t believe it, because if there were, someone would have already picked it up.

So I always look strangely at a company that says it’s in this area. It will usually be a crowded market (a red ocean), full of big, veteran companies all competing over fractions of a percent.

Examples: simple mobile apps, drop shipping, the world of advertising.

  • Pros: a fast track to acquisition by one of the companies already in the field.
  • Cons: competition isn’t healthy for a business, certainly not against veterans.

What’s next

Two follow-ups I’d like to write and hope I remember: movement between quadrants, because the market is dynamic and companies keep moving along the axes, and how we used this framework to rule out ideas very early, because we knew up front we wanted to live in quadrant 1.

This has been sitting in my head for a long time and I wanted to put it on paper, because I really think it gives people tools to evaluate ideas and their potential. Whether that’s for choosing a workplace, or for when a friend comes to you at a bar with “the next unicorn, bro”.

entry.title: Phantom features
entry.content:
The cheapest way to find out if anyone actually wants it.

Building a product, or even a feature, is expensive. It takes a lot of time and money, and most of the time your assumption about what users need is wrong. When you’re short on time and money (the definition of a startup?) you have to find a shortcut.

So what do you do?

1. Ask users whether they need it. You can, but it’s usually not enough. Users don’t really know what they want, and they’ll say “yes” because why not, especially if the product is offered for free. Experienced people will tell you the distance between saying “yes, I’d buy it” and pulling out a credit card and paying is the distance between heaven and earth.

2. Build an MVP and test it. You can, but it’s not a hit. First because it takes quite a bit of time and money. And second, when the MVP crashes and doesn’t attract users, you will always start finding excuses, because you’re already invested (“it doesn’t have all the features”, “it needs another explanation screen”, “it needs more design”), and you’ll try to make it work.

3. And my favorite: a phantom feature. I have no idea if that’s the official name. You let the user think there’s really something there, take them through the whole flow, and then say “good to know, we’ll get back to you”. That way you’re actually testing on real users.

What does that look like in practice? Eytan Levit once told a story about doing something like this at Mixtiles. They wanted to test a new product, so they built a real landing page with a purchase page, launched an ad campaign and everything. At the end they told users the product was out of stock (and gave them some compensation). That way they could simply test the product’s economic viability.
